analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.25 and expands tax credits for working parents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to two House committees in June 1989 and parked in a subcommittee that July, it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in steps from $3.35 to $4.25 an hour by 1992, and expanded the earned income tax credit for working families, paying extra for each young or school-age child. It also made concessions to employers: it let them count a larger share of workers' tips toward the minimum wage, and exempted more small businesses from coverage. It was referred to two committees, then sent to a subcommittee on labor standards, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would earn up to $4.25 an hour by 1992, and working families with children would get a larger earned income tax credit: a bigger credit rate, more income counted toward it, a minimum benefit, and inflation indexing after 1992.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage from $3.35 to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992 and after.

Expands the earned income tax credit: more earned income qualifies, the basic rate rises from 14% to 15%, and families get an extra 5% per school-age child and 10% per preschool child, up to four children.
Adds a minimum benefit so the credit does not vanish as income rises, phases it down only above $40,000 of income, and indexes credit amounts to inflation starting in 1992.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers would pay higher wages; tipped-service employers partly offset that through a larger tip credit, and businesses with under $500,000 in annual sales would drop out of minimum wage coverage, with their workers keeping only the old $3.35 floor.

drawbacks.text: The tip credit rises from 40% to 45% in 1990 and 50% after, letting employers count more of a tipped worker's tips toward the minimum wage, which reduces the cash wage the employer must pay tipped workers.

Raising the small-business coverage threshold to $500,000 in annual sales exempts more employers from the higher minimum wage; workers at newly exempt firms keep only the old $3.35 floor, so the raise does not reach everyone.

The bill limits the dependent care tax credit for children under 13 unless they cannot care for themselves, and requires parents to choose between the dependent care credit and the new earned income credit for a young child, which could reduce tax help for some working parents who pay for child care.
The phaseout scales the credit down for families with income above $40,000, so the biggest gains go to lower-income households, but the added per-child percentages sunset at four children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and sizable: a 27% minimum wage increase by 1992 plus a meaningfully larger working-family tax credit. The concessions to employers blunt the worker benefit at the edges, tipped workers see more of their pay reclassified as tips, and some small-firm workers never reach the new floor. On balance the trade is one a worker-friendly bill usually makes to win employer support: it gives up some coverage and tip-credit ground in exchange for a wage path and a bigger credit.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to a labor standards subcommittee in July 1989, it never got a hearing or a floor vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 5, 1989, by Rep. Timothy Penny with Reps. Stenholm and McCurdy, and was referred the same day to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees.
On July 12, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards in the Education and Labor Committee, the last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action appears in the record; the Congress ended January 3, 1991 with the bill still in subcommittee.

Low-wage workers were not left empty-handed: the same Congress passed a separate minimum wage bill in November 1989 that President George H.W. Bush signed, raising the wage to $4.25 by 1991 with similar tip-credit and small-business accommodations, so the practical loss from this bill's death was small.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage workers lost little in the end, because a separate minimum wage bill became law later in 1989 with a similar $4.25 target. What died with this bill was its larger earned income tax credit expansion for working parents; employers who preferred the narrower enacted package came out ahead on that piece.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; a similar wage raise passed anyway

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and all 7 cosponsors were Democrats, but it never reached a vote, so the parties' positions were never recorded.

industries.note: The bill raises the tip credit from 40% to 50% of the minimum wage, letting these employers count half the wage floor as tips and pay less cash out of pocket even as the wage rises. The mechanism shifts part of the cost of the increase onto tipped workers' cash pay.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000, removing newly small firms from minimum wage and overtime coverage. Their workers keep only the old $3.35 floor, so a gain for the firm is a loss for those employees.

Covered employers would pay up to $4.25 an hour by 1992, a 27% increase, with overtime rules unchanged. The bill's tax credits for working families partially offset the burden on the workers' side of the ledger, but the wage mandate itself is a direct cost.
